title: 16. Presentation of Data in Tabular Form

q.t: What is the class mark of the class 20–30?
q.e: The class mark is the midpoint of the class.

q.t: What is the class size of 20–30?
q.e: Upper limit − lower limit.

q.t: The number of times an observation occurs is its:
q.e: Frequency counts how often.

q.t: Find the range of 3, 8, 12, 5 and 20.
q.e: Largest − smallest.

q.t: Data collected by the investigator personally for a definite purpose is called:
q.e: It is first-hand, so it is original and reliable for that purpose.

q.t: Data taken from someone else’s records or publications is called:
q.e: It has already been collected by another person.

q.t: What is the upper limit of the class 35–45?
q.e: The value where the class ends.

q.t: For the continuous classes 10–20 and 20–30, the value 20 belongs to:
q.e: The upper limit is excluded, so every value falls in exactly one class.

q.t: A cumulative frequency is:
q.e: Each one adds the frequencies of all the classes up to that point.

q.t: Arranging data into classes with their frequencies gives a:
q.e: It shows how the observations are distributed over the classes.

q.t: The class marks of a distribution are 12, 18, 24, … What is the class size?
q.e: Consecutive class marks differ by the class size.

q.t: The class marks are 12, 18, 24, … What is the first class?
q.e: Half the size (3) on each side of 12.

q.t: Frequencies of four classes are 4, 6, 10 and 5. What is the cumulative frequency of the third class?
Frequencies of four classes are 4, 6, 10 and 5. How many observations are there?
q.e: The total of all frequencies.

q.t: The classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39 are made continuous. The first class becomes:
q.e: The gap between 19 and 20 is 1; move each limit by half of it.

q.t: After the classes 10–19, 20–29, … are made continuous, what is the class size?
The highest value is 85 and the lowest is 22. Using classes of size 7, how many classes are needed?
q.e: Range = 63, and 63 ÷ 7 = 9.

q.t: A class has class mark 35 and class size 10. What are its limits?
q.e: 5 either side of 35.

q.t: The cumulative frequency of the last class is equal to:
q.e: By then every frequency has been added.

q.t: In the data 2, 4, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2, what is the frequency of 4?
q.e: 4 occurs three times.

q.t: Cumulative frequencies: less than 10: 5; less than 20: 12; less than 30: 22; less than 40: 30. Find the frequency of the class 20–30.
q.e: Subtract the previous cumulative frequency: 22 − 12.

q.t: Cumulative frequencies: less than 10: 5; less than 20: 12; less than 30: 22; less than 40: 30. Find the frequency of the class 10–20.
Cumulative frequencies: less than 10: 5; less than 20: 12; less than 30: 22; less than 40: 30. How many observations are 20 or more?
q.e: Total 30 minus the 12 below 20.

q.t: A class has mid-value 42 and class size 10. What is its lower limit?
q.e: Half the size below the mid-value.

q.t: ‘More than’ cumulative frequencies: more than 0: 40; more than 10: 32; more than 20: 18. Find the frequency of the class 10–20.
q.e: Those above 10 but not above 20: 32 − 18.

q.t: What are the true class limits (boundaries) of the class 15–19 in the series 10–14, 15–19, 20–24?
q.e: Subtract 0.5 from the lower limit and add 0.5 to the upper.

q.t: What is the class size of the class 0.5–5.5?
Class marks are 6.5, 10.5, 14.5. What is the upper limit of the first class?
q.e: Class size 4, so half of it (2) above 6.5.

q.t: A distribution has 60 observations and 22 of them are less than 30. How many are 30 or more?
The range of a data set is 98 and it is to be grouped into 10 classes. What whole-number class size should be used?
q.e: 98 ÷ 10 = 9.8, rounded up so that the classes cover all the data.

q.t: Four classes have frequencies x, 2x, 3x and 4x, and the total is 50. Find the largest frequency.
The cumulative frequencies of five classes are 5, 13, 28, 40 and 50. What is the largest class frequency?
q.e: The frequencies are 5, 8, 15, 12, 10.

q.t: The cumulative frequencies of five classes are 5, 13, 28, 40 and 50. In which class (1st to 5th) does the 25th observation lie?
q.e: The first two classes hold 13 observations and the first three hold 28, so the 25th is in the third.

q.t: Class marks are 25, 35 and 45. What is the upper limit of the last class?
q.e: Class size 10, so the classes are 20–30, 30–40, 40–50.

q.t: In a distribution of 80 observations, the cumulative frequency just before a class is 34 and the class has frequency 18. How many observations lie ABOVE this class?
In a ‘less than’ table, the entry for ‘less than 40’ is 46 and for ‘less than 50’ is 60. What percent of the 80 observations lie in the class 40–50?
Classes 100–120, 120–140, 140–160 are used. In which class does the value 140 go?
q.e: The upper limit is excluded.

q.t: The class marks of a distribution are 47, 52, 57, 62. What are the limits of the class with mark 57?
q.e: Class size 5, so 2.5 either side.

q.t: Three classes have frequencies in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5 and the middle class has 12 observations. Find the total.
q.e: One part is 4, and there are 10 parts.

q.t: A ‘less than’ cumulative table reads 8, 20, 35, 44, 50. How many observations lie in the middle three classes together?
q.e: Up to the fourth class there are 44; remove the 8 in the first class.
